==Problem==
The smallest number greater than 2 that leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 3, 4, 5, or 6 lies between what numbers?

<imath> \textbf{(A)}\hspace{.05in}40\text{ and }50\qquad\textbf{(B)}\hspace{.05in}51\text{ and }55\qquad\textbf{(C)}\hspace{.05in}56\text{ and }60\qquad\textbf{(D)}\hspace{.05in}61\text{ and }65\qquad\textbf{(E)}\hspace{.05in}66\text{ and }99 </imath>

==Solution==
To find the answer to this problem, we need to find the least common multiple of <imath>3</imath>, <imath>4</imath>, <imath>5</imath>, <imath>6</imath> and add <imath>2</imath> to the result. To calculate the least common multiple, we need to find the prime factorization for each of them. <imath>3 = 3^{1}</imath>, <imath>4 = 2^{2}</imath>, <imath>5 = 5^{1}</imath>, and <imath>6 = 2^{1}*{3^{1}}</imath>. So the least common multiple of the four numbers is <imath>2^{2}*{3^{1}*{5^{1}}} = 60</imath>, and by adding <imath>2</imath>, we find that that such number is <imath>62</imath>. Now we need to find the only given range that contains <imath>62</imath>. The only such range is answer <imath>\textbf{(D)}</imath>, and so our final answer is <imath> \boxed{\textbf{(D)}\ 61\text{ and }65} </imath>.

~NXC

==Solution 2(Chinese Remainder Theorem)==
We have to find the smallest number <imath>x</imath> for <imath>x \equiv 2\mod3</imath>, <imath>x \equiv 2\mod4</imath>, and <imath>x \equiv 2\mod5</imath>. We are excluding six because it won't make our divisors relatively prime. For the first equation, <imath>x \equiv 2\mod3</imath> holds remainder(<imath>r</imath>) of 2. Now we have to find <imath>M</imath>. Our <imath>M</imath> which is all divisors multiplied by each other divided by the divisor we are using. So our <imath>M</imath> is <imath>\frac{3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5}{3}=20</imath>. We now need to find the inverse of <imath>a</imath> times <imath>M</imath> and solve <imath>a</imath>. Doing this we can get <imath>20a \equiv 1\mod3</imath>, and the smallest value of <imath>a</imath> where this is true is <imath>2</imath>. Now we multiply every value we have which gets us <imath>2 \cdot 20 \cdot 2</imath>. Then we repeat for mod 4 and mod 5. For mod 4 the numbers <imath>r</imath>,<imath>M</imath>,<imath>a</imath> are <imath>2</imath>, <imath>15</imath>, and <imath>3</imath> respectively. For mod 5 we get <imath>2</imath>,<imath>12</imath>, and <imath>8</imath>. Now we have to multiply all our values and we get <imath>80</imath> (mod 3), <imath>90</imath> (mod 4), and <imath>192</imath> (mod 5). Now we do <imath>80+90+192\mod{5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3}</imath>. This is <imath>362\mod60</imath>. This means <imath>x \equiv 2\mod60</imath>, but since it needs to be greater than <imath>2</imath>, we get <imath>62</imath>, which divided by six also has a remainder of 2. So <imath>62</imath> is in the range of <imath> \boxed{\textbf{(D)}\ 61\text{ and }65} </imath>.

==Solution 2(Chinese Remainder Theorem-Method algebric)==

Let <imath>x</imath> the number of problem. 

By Chinese Remainder Theorem, we know that

<imath>\begin{cases} 
x \equiv 2 \pmod 3 \\
x \equiv 2 \pmod 4 \\
x \equiv 2 \pmod 5 
\end{cases}</imath>

<imath>x \equiv 2 \pmod 6</imath> is exclude because it won't make our divisors relatively prime. 
The solution in this problem is:

<cmath>x \equiv  \sum^{n=3}_{k=1} a_kb_kc_k \pmod {4 \times 3 \times 5} \implies x\equiv  \sum^{n=3}_{k=1} a_kb_kc_k \pmod {60}</cmath>

where:

<imath>a_k: \text {The product of all moduli except the k-th modulus.}</imath>

<imath>b_k: \text{Inverse modular}</imath>

<imath>c_k: \text{remainder of x by k-th modulus}</imath>

Since the <imath>c_1=c_2=c_3=2</imath>:

<cmath> a_1=\frac{3\times 4 \times 5}{3} = 20 \implies 20b_1 \equiv 1 \pmod 3 \implies 2b_1 \equiv 1 \pmod 3 \therefore b_1=2</cmath>


<cmath> a_2=\frac{3\times 4 \times 5}{4} = 15 \implies 15b_2 \equiv 1 \pmod 4 \implies 3b_2 \equiv 1 \pmod 4 \therefore b_2=3</cmath>


<cmath> a_3=\frac{3\times 4 \times 5}{5} = 12 \implies 12b_2 \equiv 1 \pmod 5 \implies 2b_2 \equiv 1 \pmod 5 \therefore b_3=3</cmath>

therefore

<cmath> x\equiv  \sum^{n=3}_{k=1} a_kb_kc_k \pmod {60} \Rightarrow x\equiv 20 \times 2 \times 2 + 15 \times 2 \times 3 + 12 \times 2 \times 3\pmod {60} \Rightarrow x\equiv  242 \pmod {60} \Rightarrow x\equiv  2 \pmod {60} </cmath>

Thus, <imath>x=60m+2>2 \implies m>0</imath> and for <imath>m=1 \implies x=62</imath>. 

Correct answer: <imath>\boxed{D}</imath>
